Q#200 Sec 1: Low-Code AI
General ML NB ≠ Vote (A)
scanned from paper-based customer feedback formsEvery form has the same layoutoverall satisfaction score from the customer comments
Clue: Extracting text from a specific region of fixed-layout scanned PDF forms requires Document AI Custom Extractor, and predicting an overall document sentiment score requires Natural Language API analyzeSentiment.
View Full Question & 4 Options

You work for a hotel and have a dataset that contains customers’ written comments scanned from paper-based customer feedback forms, which are stored as PDF files. Every form has the same layout. You need to quickly predict an overall satisfaction score from the customer comments on each form. How should you accomplish this task?

• Option A: Use the Vision API to parse the text from each PDF file. Use the Natural Language API analyzeSentiment feature to infer overall satisfaction scores.
• Option B: Use the Vision API to parse the text from each PDF file. Use the Natural Language API analyzeEntitySentiment feature to infer overall satisfaction scores.
✓ Option C: Uptrain a Document AI custom extractor to parse the text in the comments section of each PDF file. Use the Natural Language API analyzeSentiment feature to infer overall satisfaction scores.
• Option D: Uptrain a Document AI custom extractor to parse the text in the comments section of each PDF file. Use the Natural Language API analyzeEntitySentiment feature to infer overall satisfaction scores.
Final Key: C
📓 NB & Gemini: CVote: A

Uptraining a Document AI custom extractor isolates the specific comments section on fixed-layout forms, and Natural Language API analyzeSentiment computes the overall satisfaction score.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Document AI Custom Extractor & Cloud Natural Language API Sentiment Analysis)
✅ Why C is Correct: Because all scanned PDF feedback forms share a fixed layout containing form headers, prompts, and other fields alongside the written comments box, uptraining a Document AI Custom Extractor isolates only the specific `comments` region cleanly, and Cloud Natural Language API `analyzeSentiment` computes the overall document satisfaction score. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Cloud Vision API OCR extracts all text across the entire PDF page indiscriminately (mixing form instructions, scales, and boilerplate with customer comments), skewing overall sentiment scores. • B: Vision API fails to isolate the `comments` field, and `analyzeEntitySentiment` extracts per-entity sentiment rather than a single overall satisfaction score. • D: `analyzeEntitySentiment` computes sentiment toward individual named nouns/entities rather than inferring one overall customer satisfaction score for the comment.
  • × A Vision API performs full-page generic OCR and cannot isolate only the comments section from other form text.
  • × B Vision API lacks field-specific form extraction, and analyzeEntitySentiment targets individual nouns rather than overall satisfaction.
  • × D Natural Language API analyzeEntitySentiment evaluates sentiment per entity rather than producing a single overall satisfaction score.
Q#201 Sec 5: ML Pipelines
Vertex AI
Vertex AI pipelinemany model iterations by adjusting the code and parameters of the training stephigh costs associated with the development, particularly the data export and preprocessing steps
Clue: Vertex AI Pipelines step caching relies on deterministic component YAML specifications; injecting dynamic timestamps into upstream component filenames invalidates the cache on every run.
View Full Question & 4 Options

You developed a Vertex AI pipeline that trains a classification model on data stored in a large BigQuery table. The pipeline has four steps, where each step is created by a Python function that uses the KubeFlow v2 API. The components have the following names: You launch your Vertex AI pipeline as the following: You perform many model iterations by adjusting the code and parameters of the training step. You observe high costs associated with the development, particularly the data export and preprocessing steps. You need to reduce model development costs. What should you do?

✓ Option A: Change the components’ YAML filenames to export.yaml, preprocess,yaml, f "train- {dt}.yaml", f"calibrate-{dt).vaml".
• Option B: Add the {"kubeflow.v1.caching": True} parameter to the set of params provided to your PipelineJob.
• Option C: Move the first step of your pipeline to a separate step, and provide a cached path to Cloud Storage as an input to the main pipeline.
• Option D: Change the name of the pipeline to f"my-awesome-pipeline-{dt}".
Final Key: A
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (A)

Using static YAML filenames (export.yaml, preprocess.yaml) for unchanged upstream steps preserves their component hashes so Vertex AI Pipelines can reuse cached outputs.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex AI Pipelines Execution Caching & KFP v2 Component Compilation)
✅ Why A is Correct: As shown in the pipeline code snippet (`enable_caching=True` is already enabled on `PipelineJob`), embedding a dynamic timestamp `{dt}` into `f'export-{dt}.yaml'` and `f'preprocess-{dt}.yaml'` changes the compiled component spec/name on every run and invalidates KFP v2 cache lookup; switching them to static `export.yaml` and `preprocess.yaml` lets Vertex AI Pipelines reuse cached BigQuery export and preprocessing outputs while re-running modified `train` and `calibrate` steps. ❌ Why Others Fail: • B: `enable_caching=True` is already set on `PipelineJob` in the snippet, and `{"kubeflow.v1.caching": True}` is not a valid Vertex AI Pipelines parameter. • C: Manually splitting out only the export step into a separate pipeline leaves the expensive preprocessing step uncached and adds manual GCS path management when native KFP caching handles both automatically. • D: Changing the pipeline name to include `{dt}` does not fix the dynamic component specs that invalidate task-level cache keys.
  • × B Kubeflow v2 caching is enabled via enable_caching=True on PipelineJob, not via a v1 dictionary parameter.
  • × C Manually splitting the pipeline and passing static GCS paths breaks end-to-end lineage and adds unnecessary manual overhead.
  • × D Changing the pipeline run name does not fix cache invalidation caused by dynamic timestamps in component YAML filenames.

You work for a startup that has multiple data science workloads. Your compute infrastructure is currently on-premises, and the data science workloads are native to PySpark. Your team plans to migrate their data science workloads to Google Cloud. You need to build a proof of concept to migrate one data science job to Google Cloud. You want to propose a migration process that requires minimal cost and effort. What should you do first?

• Option A: Create a n2-standard-4 VM instance and install Java, Scala, and Apache Spark dependencies on it.
• Option B: Create a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster with a basic node pool configuration, install Java, Scala, and Apache Spark dependencies on it.
✓ Option C: Create a Standard (1 master, 3 workers) Dataproc cluster, and run a Vertex AI Workbench notebook instance on it.
• Option D: Create a Vertex AI Workbench notebook with instance type n2-standard-4.
Final Key: C
📓 NB & Gemini: CVote: D

Provisioning a Standard Dataproc cluster with a Vertex AI Workbench notebook instance provides a fully managed, pre-configured PySpark environment for rapid migration.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Cloud Dataproc & Vertex AI Workbench Dataproc Integration) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 §2
✅ Why C is Correct: Cloud Dataproc is Google Cloud's managed Apache Spark service purpose-built for lift-and-shift migration of on-premises PySpark workloads—provisioning a Standard cluster (1 master, 3 workers) in under 90 seconds with Spark/Java/Scala preconfigured and running a Dataproc-backed Vertex AI Workbench notebook validates an authentic distributed PySpark migration process with minimal effort. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Manually installing and maintaining Java, Scala, and Apache Spark on a raw Compute Engine VM incurs unnecessary sysadmin effort and only tests single-node execution. • B: Configuring a GKE cluster and manually installing Java, Scala, and Spark dependencies introduces high Kubernetes operational complexity and overhead. • D: A standalone `n2-standard-4` Vertex AI Workbench VM is a single 4-vCPU Python deep learning VM without a distributed Spark cluster, so it neither validates distributed PySpark behavior nor establishes a repeatable cluster migration path for multiple on-prem Spark workloads.
  • × A Manually installing Java, Scala, and Spark on a standalone Compute Engine VM incurs high setup effort and lacks cluster scalability.
  • × B Deploying and configuring Apache Spark manually on GKE adds significant operational and Kubernetes management overhead.
  • × D A standalone Vertex AI Workbench VM without a Dataproc cluster lacks distributed Spark workers for native PySpark cluster workloads.

You work for a bank. You have been asked to develop an ML model that will support loan application decisions. You need to determine which Vertex AI services to include in the workflow. You want to track the model’s training parameters and the metrics per training epoch. You plan to compare the performance of each version of the model to determine the best model based on your chosen metrics. Which Vertex AI services should you use?

• Option A: Vertex ML Metadata, Vertex AI Feature Store, and Vertex AI Vizier
• Option B: Vertex AI Pipelines, Vertex AI Experiments, and Vertex AI Vizier
✓ Option C: Vertex ML Metadata, Vertex AI Experiments, and Vertex AI TensorBoard
• Option D: Vertex AI Pipelines, Vertex AI Feature Store, and Vertex AI TensorBoard
Final Key: C
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (C)

Vertex ML Metadata logs parameters and lineage, Vertex AI Experiments compares model runs, and Vertex AI TensorBoard visualizes metrics per training epoch.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex ML Metadata, Vertex AI Experiments, & Vertex AI TensorBoard)
✅ Why C is Correct: Vertex ML Metadata records training parameters and artifact lineage for banking auditability, Vertex AI TensorBoard tracks and visualizes loss/metrics per training epoch, and Vertex AI Experiments compares run parameters and evaluation metrics across model versions to select the best model. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Vertex AI Feature Store manages feature storage/serving and Vertex AI Vizier performs black-box hyperparameter optimization; neither provides per-epoch training curve tracking or experiment comparison tables. • B: Vertex AI Vizier tunes hyperparameters rather than visualizing per-epoch training metrics (`Vertex AI TensorBoard`) or storing governance metadata (`Vertex ML Metadata`). • D: Omits `Vertex AI Experiments` (needed to compare model versions across chosen evaluation metrics) and includes `Vertex AI Feature Store`, which is unrelated to experiment tracking.
  • × A Feature Store manages features and Vizier performs hyperparameter tuning; neither visualizes epoch-by-epoch training metrics.
  • × B Pipelines orchestrates workflows and Vizier tunes hyperparameters, lacking epoch-level visualization via TensorBoard.
  • × D Feature Store and Pipelines do not provide interactive experiment run comparison like Vertex AI Experiments.

You need to quickly create an initial model. What should you do?

• Option A: Download a pre-trained object detection model from TensorFlow Hub. Fine-tune the model in Vertex AI Workbench by using the annotated image data.
✓ Option B: Train an object detection model in AutoML by using the annotated image data.
• Option C: Create a pipeline in Vertex AI Pipelines and configure the AutoMLTrainingJobRunOp component to train a custom object detection model by using the annotated image data.
• Option D: Train an object detection model in Vertex AI custom training by using the annotated image data.
Final Key: B
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (B)

Training an AutoML object detection model on the annotated dataset delivers a rapid, codeless baseline for bounding-box detection.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex AI AutoML Image Object Detection) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 §1.1
✅ Why B is Correct: With bounding-box annotations and class labels already assembled and a sufficient cloud budget, Vertex AI AutoML Image Object Detection is the fastest, no-code path to train and evaluate a high-quality baseline damaged-part detector for a proof of concept. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Manually downloading a TensorFlow Hub detector and writing fine-tuning, data-loading, and evaluation scripts in Vertex AI Workbench takes significantly longer than AutoML. • C: Authoring and compiling a Vertex AI Pipeline (`AutoMLImageTrainingJobRunOp`, misnamed `AutoMLTrainingJobRunOp` here) adds unnecessary MLOps orchestration overhead for a one-off initial PoC baseline. • D: Writing custom object detection training code and containerizing a Vertex AI Custom Training job requires substantial engineering time compared to AutoML.
  • × A Fine-tuning a TensorFlow Hub model in Workbench requires writing custom training and data-loading code, slowing down PoC delivery.
  • × C Building an automated Vertex AI Pipeline is unnecessary engineering overhead for a one-off initial proof-of-concept model.
  • × D Vertex AI custom training requires developing and containerizing custom object detection code rather than quickly training a baseline.
Q#205 Sec 2: Data & Collab
General ML GenAI / LLM
healthcare organizationpersonally identifiable information (PII)perform data exploration and preprocessing while ensuring the security and privacy of sensitive fields
Clue: Protecting sensitive PII from exposure to analysts during exploratory data analysis requires de-identification via Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Sensitive Data Protection) prior to analysis.
View Full Question & 4 Options

You are analyzing customer data for a healthcare organization that is stored in Cloud Storage. The data contains personally identifiable information (PII). You need to perform data exploration and preprocessing while ensuring the security and privacy of sensitive fields. What should you do?

✓ Option A: Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API to de-identify the PII before performing data exploration and preprocessing.
• Option B: Use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) to encrypt the PII data at rest, and decrypt the PII data during data exploration and preprocessing.
• Option C: Use a VM inside a VPC Service Controls security perimeter to perform data exploration and preprocessing.
• Option D: Use Google-managed encryption keys to encrypt the PII data at rest, and decrypt the PII data during data exploration and preprocessing.
Final Key: A
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (A)

Using the Cloud DLP API to redact, mask, or tokenize PII before exploration ensures sensitive healthcare fields are never exposed in plaintext.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Sensitive Data Protection / Cloud DLP De-identification) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 §2
✅ Why A is Correct: Using Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP / Sensitive Data Protection) API to inspect and de-identify (redact, mask, or cryptographic-hash/tokenize) PII fields before data exploration ensures sensitive healthcare identifiers are never exposed in cleartext to analysts or downstream ML models. ❌ Why Others Fail: • B: CMEK protects storage media at rest, but explicitly decrypting the PII during exploration exposes raw sensitive healthcare identifiers to users. • C: VPC Service Controls block unauthorized data exfiltration outside the network perimeter, but do not mask or de-identify cleartext PII fields viewed by analysts inside the perimeter. • D: Google-managed encryption at rest automatically decrypts objects upon authorized read, leaving all raw PII visible during exploration and preprocessing.
  • × B CMEK only encrypts data at rest; decrypting it during exploration exposes raw PII to the user.
  • × C VPC Service Controls prevent network exfiltration but do not mask or hide raw PII fields from analysts reading the data.
  • × D Google-managed encryption at rest still exposes plaintext PII once decrypted for data exploration and preprocessing.

Model Development
predictive maintenance modelhigh definition images of the bridges as model inputsexplain the output of the model
Clue: High-definition image inputs require a differentiable deep learning model (TensorFlow) paired with gradient-based pixel attribution (Integrated Gradients).
View Full Question & 4 Options

You are building a predictive maintenance model to preemptively detect part defects in bridges. You plan to use high definition images of the bridges as model inputs. You need to explain the output of the model to the relevant stakeholders so they can take appropriate action. How should you build the model?

• Option A: Use scikit-learn to build a tree-based model, and use SHAP values to explain the model output.
• Option B: Use scikit-learn to build a tree-based model, and use partial dependence plots (PDP) to explain the model output.
✓ Option C: Use TensorFlow to create a deep learning-based model, and use Integrated Gradients to explain the model output.
• Option D: Use TensorFlow to create a deep learning-based model, and use the sampled Shapley method to explain the model output.
Final Key: C
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (C)

Building a TensorFlow deep learning model and using Integrated Gradients efficiently computes pixel-level feature attributions for high-definition images.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex Explainable AI: Integrated Gradients vs Sampled Shapley)
✅ Why C is Correct: High-definition bridge inspection images require a differentiable deep convolutional/vision neural network in TensorFlow, and Integrated Gradients computes pixel-level feature attributions along the gradient path efficiently—highlighting the exact defective bridge regions for stakeholders. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: `scikit-learn` tree models cannot effectively learn spatial representations over high-definition raw images without manual feature extraction. • B: Tree-based `scikit-learn` models and global Partial Dependence Plots (PDPs) are designed for low-dimensional tabular features, not pixel-level explanations on high-definition images. • D: In Vertex Explainable AI, Sampled Shapley permutes discrete input features and is intended for tabular models; it is computationally intractable and unsuited for high-definition pixel grids compared to Integrated Gradients or XRAI.
  • × A Scikit-learn tree-based models are unsuitable for raw high-definition image classification.
  • × B Tree-based models and partial dependence plots (PDP) are designed for tabular features, not raw pixel arrays.
  • × D Sampled Shapley is computationally inefficient for high-dimensional image pixels compared to Integrated Gradients.

You work for a hospital that wants to optimize how it schedules operations. You need to create a model that uses the relationship between the number of surgeries scheduled and beds used. You want to predict how many beds will be needed for patients each day in advance based on the scheduled surgeries. You have one year of data for the hospital organized in 365 rows. The data includes the following variables for each day: • Number of scheduled surgeries • Number of beds occupied • Date You want to maximize the speed of model development and testing. What should you do?

✓ Option A: Create a BigQuery table. Use BigQuery ML to build a regression model, with number of beds as the target variable, and number of scheduled surgeries and date features (such as day of week) as the predictors.
• Option B: Create a BigQuery table. Use BigQuery ML to build an ARIMA model, with number of beds as the target variable, and date as the time variable.
• Option C: Create a Vertex AI tabular dataset. Train an AutoML regression model, with number of beds as the target variable, and number of scheduled minor surgeries and date features (such as day of the week) as the predictors.
• Option D: Create a Vertex AI tabular dataset. Train a Vertex AI AutoML Forecasting model, with number of beds as the target variable, number of scheduled surgeries as a covariate and date as the time variable.
Final Key: A
📓 NB: AGemini: DVote: D

Create a BigQuery table. Use BigQuery ML to build a regression model, with number of beds as the target variable, and number of scheduled surgeries and date features (such as day of week) as the predictors. — With only 365 daily rows, BigQuery ML regression (`LINEAR_REG` or `BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR`) trains and evaluates in seconds directly via SQL while modeling `beds occupied` from `scheduled surgeries` and calendar predictors (such as day of week)—maximizing development and testing speed without hitting AutoML's minimum row limit.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex AI AutoML Tabular 1,000-Row Minimum Quota & BigQuery ML Regression)
✅ Why A is Correct: With only 365 daily rows, BigQuery ML regression (`LINEAR_REG` or `BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR`) trains and evaluates in seconds directly via SQL while modeling `beds occupied` from `scheduled surgeries` and calendar predictors (such as day of week)—maximizing development and testing speed without hitting AutoML's minimum row limit. ❌ Why Others Fail: • B: Standard BigQuery ML `ARIMA` (`MODEL_TYPE='ARIMA'` / univariate `ARIMA_PLUS` using only `beds` and `date`) forecasts purely from historical bed counts and ignores `Number of scheduled surgeries`, losing the primary causal predictor. • C: Vertex AI AutoML Tabular Regression enforces a strict minimum dataset requirement of 1,000 rows (so a 365-row dataset fails validation immediately), takes hours to train, and only references minor surgeries. • D: Vertex AI AutoML Forecasting also enforces a hard minimum of 1,000 rows (`prepare-data` quota: 1,000 to 100,000,000 rows)—rejecting a 365-row dataset—and requires multi-hour neural architecture search/training rather than rapid testing.
  • × B Standard BigQuery ML `ARIMA` (`MODEL_TYPE='ARIMA'` / univariate `ARIMA_PLUS` using only `beds` and `date`) forecasts purely from historical bed counts and ignores `Number of scheduled surgeries`, losing the primary causal predictor.
  • × C Vertex AI AutoML Tabular Regression enforces a strict minimum dataset requirement of 1,000 rows (so a 365-row dataset fails validation immediately), takes hours to train, and only references minor surgeries.
  • × D Vertex AI AutoML Forecasting also enforces a hard minimum of 1,000 rows (`prepare-data` quota: 1,000 to 100,000,000 rows)—rejecting a 365-row dataset—and requires multi-hour neural architecture search/training rather than rapid testing.

Using KFP with BigQueryJobOp reuses the existing SQL preprocessing script directly, and CustomTrainingJobOp runs the TensorFlow model on Vertex AI.

✅ Why A is Correct: Official Cloud TPU documentation specifies that TPUs are unsuitable for models containing custom TensorFlow C++ operations inside the main training loop, requiring NVIDIA GPUs instead; using 8 `a2-megagpu-16g` workers (128 A100 GPUs total with 16-GPU intra-node NVSwitch and high GPUDirect-TCPX bandwidth) with `MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy` halves inter-node network hops compared to 16 8-GPU nodes, minimizing multi-week training time and total compute cost. ❌ Why Others Fail: • B: Cloud TPUs compile training loops via XLA and do not support arbitrary custom TensorFlow operations inside the `tf.function` training step without falling back to host CPU, severely bottlenecking or failing execution. • C: CPU-only `c2d-highcpu-32` VMs cannot feasibly pretrain a large language model, and `tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy` is a single-worker strategy rather than a 16-worker cluster strategy. • D: Spreading the same 128 A100 GPUs across twice as many VMs (`16 × a2-highgpu-8g` vs `8 × a2-megagpu-16g`) doubles inter-node network synchronization overhead for large-batch `MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy` all-reduce, slowing training and increasing total cost.

  • × C CPU-only machines (c2d-highcpu-32) are orders of magnitude too slow for LLM pre-training, and MirroredStrategy is for single-node training.

Q#225 Sec 6: Monitoring AI
BigQuery ML GenAI / LLM
predict which customers may fail to pay their next phone billproactively offer at-risk customers assistanceinvestigate and mitigate potential bias against disadvantaged groups, while preserving model accuracy
Clue: Evaluating fairness for an assistive intervention requires retaining predictive features to preserve accuracy and measuring group fairness metrics (accuracy/recall parity across sensitive attributes) on test predictions.
View Full Question & 4 Options

You work for a telecommunications company. You’re building a model to predict which customers may fail to pay their next phone bill. The purpose of this model is to proactively offer at-risk customers assistance such as service discounts and bill deadline extensions. The data is stored in BigQuery and the predictive features that are available for model training include: - Customer_id - Age - Salary (measured in local currency) - Sex - Average bill value (measured in local currency) - Number of phone calls in the last month (integer) - Average duration of phone calls (measured in minutes) You need to investigate and mitigate potential bias against disadvantaged groups, while preserving model accuracy. What should you do?

• Option A: Determine whether there is a meaningful correlation between the sensitive features and the other features. Train a BigQuery ML boosted trees classification model and exclude the sensitive features and any meaningfully correlated features.
• Option B: Train a BigQuery ML boosted trees classification model with all features. Use the ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN method to calculate the global attribution values for each feature of the model. If the feature importance value for any of the sensitive features exceeds a threshold, discard the model and tram without this feature.
• Option C: Train a BigQuery ML boosted trees classification model with all features. Use the ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT method to calculate the attribution values for each feature for each customer in a test set. If for any individual customer, the importance value for any feature exceeds a predefined threshold, discard the model and train the model again without this feature.
✓ Option D: Define a fairness metric that is represented by accuracy across the sensitive features. Train a BigQuery ML boosted trees classification model with all features. Use the trained model to make predictions on a test set. Join the data back with the sensitive features, and calculate a fairness metric to investigate whether it meets your requirements.
Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Training the model with all features and joining test predictions with sensitive attributes to evaluate subgroup fairness metrics quantifies bias without blindly sacrificing accuracy.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google ML Crash Course (Fairness: Evaluating for Fairness) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 Sec 6.1 (Responsible AI & Bias)
✅ Why D is Correct: Investigating algorithmic bias requires defining quantitative fairness metrics (such as subgroup accuracy, equal opportunity, or predictive parity) and performing sliced evaluation on a held-out test set joined with sensitive demographic attributes. Keeping predictive features during training preserves accuracy—especially important for assistive interventions like bill extensions—while explicitly measuring whether subgroup performance meets fairness thresholds. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Removing sensitive features ('fairness through unawareness') along with correlated predictive features like salary and average bill value severely degrades model accuracy without guaranteeing equitable subgroup outcomes. • B: Global feature attribution (`ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN`) measures overall feature contribution to predictions rather than error-rate disparities across disadvantaged demographic slices. • C: Discarding and retraining an entire model whenever any single test customer has a high local attribution (`ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT`) conflates individual feature contribution with systemic demographic bias.
  • × A Dropping sensitive features and all correlated features ('fairness through unawareness') severely degrades model accuracy without guaranteeing fair outcomes.
  • × B Global feature importance only shows average reliance on a feature, not whether disadvantaged groups suffer disparate error rates.
  • × C Discarding a model because a single customer has high local feature attribution is statistically invalid and does not measure group fairness.

You work for a manufacturing company. You need to train a custom image classification model to detect product defects at the end of an assembly line. What should you do?

Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex Explainable AI — Example-Based Explanations Overview)
✅ Why D is Correct: Vertex Explainable AI's example-based explanations retrieve the nearest neighbors from the training dataset in the model's internal latent space (configured by specifying the custom image model's embedding output layer). This directly diagnoses high-confidence holdout misclassifications by revealing mislabeled or visually ambiguous training examples. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Pixel-level Integrated Gradients highlights saliency regions on the test image itself, which cannot expose mislabeled ground-truth examples inside the training set. • B: Standalone Vertex AI Vector Search (Matching Engine) requires manually building an embedding extraction and indexing pipeline, whereas example-based explanations natively integrate latent-space nearest-neighbor retrieval into Vertex Explainable AI. • C: XRAI only provides per-image region saliency rather than training-set counterfactuals/neighbors, and `OUTLINES` is an Integrated Gradients visualization setting rather than a recommended XRAI setting.

You have deployed a scikit-team model to a Vertex AI endpoint using a custom model server. You enabled autoscaling: however, the deployed model fails to scale beyond one replica, which led to dropped requests. You notice that CPU utilization remains low even during periods of high load. What should you do?

• Option A: Attach a GPU to the prediction nodes
✓ Option B: Increase the number of workers in your model server
• Option C: Schedule scaling of the nodes to match expected demand
• Option D: Increase the minReplicaCount in your DeployedModel configuration
Final Key: B

Increasing the number of workers in the custom model server enables parallel request handling across all vCPUs, raising CPU utilization under load so autoscaling triggers properly.

Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex AI Prediction — Custom Container Requirements & Scaling Best Practices) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 Sec 4.2
✅ Why B is Correct: Vertex AI Endpoint autoscaling scales replicas based on average CPU utilization (default 60%). When a custom HTTP model server runs with only a single worker process/thread on a multi-vCPU node, requests serialize on one core while remaining cores sit idle—keeping overall CPU utilization below the scaling threshold while dropping concurrent requests. Increasing model server workers utilizes all vCPUs in parallel and allows CPU metrics to trigger autoscaling. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Attaching a GPU does not accelerate traditional CPU-bound scikit-learn inference or resolve single-worker HTTP server concurrency bottlenecks. • C: Scheduled node scaling cannot solve per-replica worker concurrency limits and adds manual operational guesswork. • D: Raising `minReplicaCount` provisions more underutilized single-worker replicas upfront at higher baseline cost without fixing the root concurrency bottleneck or broken autoscaling trigger.
  • × A Scikit-learn models run on CPUs and do not utilize GPUs without specialized libraries.
  • × C Manual scheduled scaling does not fix the underlying single-worker concurrency bottleneck on each replica.
  • × D Increasing minReplicaCount wastes idle compute and still leaves each replica bottlenecked by a single worker process.

You are developing an ML model that predicts the cost of used automobiles based on data such as location, condition, model type, color, and engine/battery efficiency. The data is updated every night. You created a Vertex AI pipeline that reads the data splits the data into training/evaluation/test sets performs feature engineering trains the model by using the training dataset and validates the model by using the evaluation dataset. You need to configure a retraining workflow that minimizes cost. What should you do?

• Option A: Compare the training and evaluation losses of the current run. If the losses are similar, deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint. Configure a cron job to redeploy the pipeline every night.
• Option B: Compare the training and evaluation losses of the current run. If the losses are similar, deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with training/serving skew threshold model monitoring. When the model monitoring threshold is triggered redeploy the pipeline.
• Option C: Compare the results to the evaluation results from a previous run. If the performance improved deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint. Configure a cron job to redeploy the pipeline every night.
✓ Option D: Compare the results to the evaluation results from a previous run. If the performance improved deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with training/serving skew threshold model monitoring. When the model monitoring threshold is triggered redeploy the pipeline.
Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Comparing candidate evaluation metrics against the previous run ensures model improvement, and triggering retraining via Vertex AI Model Monitoring skew alerts minimizes unnecessary nightly compute costs.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: PMLE Study Guide v2.0 Sec 5.1–5.2 & Sec 6.2 (Model Validation, Continuous Training Triggers, & Skew Monitoring)
✅ Why D is Correct: Proper automated model validation ('champion-challenger blessing') compares the candidate model's evaluation metrics against the previously deployed run's evaluation metrics before promotion. Deploying with Vertex AI Model Monitoring and triggering pipeline retraining only when training-serving skew exceeds a threshold minimizes unnecessary compute spend compared to blind nightly retraining. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Comparing current training vs. evaluation loss only checks for overfitting rather than improvement over the existing production model, and nightly cron retraining wastes compute when data distributions are stable. • B: Uses training-vs-evaluation loss parity instead of champion-challenger model comparison, risking deployment of a non-overfit model that performs worse than the current production model. • C: Retraining unconditionally every single night via a cron job incurs unnecessary daily training pipeline costs even when incoming car data has not shifted.
  • × A Comparing training and evaluation losses only checks for overfitting (not improvement over the current production model), and nightly cron retraining wastes compute.
  • × B Deploying whenever training and evaluation losses are similar can replace a strong production model with an equally consistent but less accurate model.
  • × C Retraining via a nightly cron job regardless of whether data distribution has shifted incurs unnecessary daily training costs.

You trained a model packaged it with a custom Docker container for serving, and deployed it to Vertex AI Model Registry. When you submit a batch prediction job, it fails with this error: "Error model server never became ready. Please validate that your model file or container configuration are valid. " There are no additional errors in the logs. What should you do?

• Option A: Add a logging configuration to your application to emit logs to Cloud Logging
• Option B: Change the HTTP port in your model’s configuration to the default value of 8080
• Option C: Change the healthRoute value in your model’s configuration to /healthcheck
✓ Option D: Pull the Docker image locally, and use the docker run command to launch it locally. Use the docker logs command to explore the error logs
Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Running the Docker container locally with docker run and inspecting docker logs immediately reveals startup crashes, missing dependencies, or entrypoint errors.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex AI Prediction — Locally Test and Troubleshoot Custom Containers) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 Sec 6.2
✅ Why D is Correct: When a custom serving container fails readiness checks on Vertex AI with no Cloud Logging entries, pulling the image and running it locally via `docker run` followed by `docker logs` immediately exposes early startup crashes (such as missing Python packages, entrypoint syntax errors, or failed model deserialization) before the HTTP server initializes. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Vertex AI automatically captures standard output (`stdout`) and standard error (`stderr`) from running containers into Cloud Logging; adding application-level logging will not help if the container crashes before starting. • B: Port 8080 is already Vertex AI's default container prediction port, and blindly changing configuration settings without diagnosing the startup crash guesses at the cause. • C: Blindly changing `healthRoute` to `/healthcheck` without knowing what route the server exposes or why startup failed will not resolve an unready container.
  • × A Vertex AI automatically captures container stdout/stderr in Cloud Logging; if no logs appear, the container crashed before starting the app.
  • × B Blindly changing the HTTP port to 8080 guesses at a configuration parameter without diagnosing why the container failed to start.
  • × C Blindly changing the healthRoute path without verifying the container's actual routes or startup failure does not identify the root cause.

You are developing an ML model to identify your company’s products in images. You have access to over one million images in a Cloud Storage bucket. You plan to experiment with different TensorFlow models by using Vertex AI Training. You need to read images at scale during training while minimizing data I/O bottlenecks. What should you do?

• Option A: Load the images directly into the Vertex AI compute nodes by using Cloud Storage FUSE. Read the images by using the tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices function
• Option B: Create a Vertex AI managed dataset from your image data. Access the AIP_TRAINING_DATA_URI environment variable to read the images by using the tf.data.Dataset.list_files function.
✓ Option C: Convert the images to TFRecords and store them in a Cloud Storage bucket. Read the TFRecords by using the tf.data.TFRecordDataset function.
• Option D: Store the URLs of the images in a CSV file. Read the file by using the tf.data.experimental.CsvDataset function.
Final Key: C
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (C)

Converting the images into sharded TFRecords in Cloud Storage and streaming them with tf.data.TFRecordDataset maximizes sequential read throughput during training.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: PMLE Study Guide v2.0 Course 07 Module 2 & Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Optimize TensorFlow Input Pipelines with TFRecords)
✅ Why C is Correct: Consolidating over one million individual images into sharded binary TFRecord files in Cloud Storage and reading them in parallel via `tf.data.TFRecordDataset` replaces millions of high-latency small-object HTTP openings per epoch with high-throughput sequential streaming, eliminating I/O bottlenecks across repeated Vertex AI Training experiments. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: `tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices` attempts to materialize tensors in memory, and reading 1M+ small individual files over Cloud Storage FUSE suffers high per-file metadata latency. • B: Using `tf.data.Dataset.list_files` over raw images in a managed dataset still issues over one million individual small-object reads from Cloud Storage on every training epoch. • D: Reading image URLs from a CSV file via `CsvDataset` still requires fetching each of the one million small image files individually over the network during training.
  • × A Mounting Cloud Storage via FUSE and reading over a million individual small image files causes high metadata latency and slow random I/O.
  • × B Using tf.data.Dataset.list_files on a million individual image objects in GCS still suffers from high per-file HTTP request overhead.
  • × D Reading image URLs from a CSV still requires fetching over a million individual image files during training.

✅ Why C is Correct: In the Vertex AI Python SDK, `log_time_series_metrics` logs step-by-step training metrics over iterations/epochs (such as training loss curves) and strictly requires associating a backing Vertex AI TensorBoard instance with the Experiment. Preprocessed datasets are tracked as lineage artifacts on the experiment execution using `assign_input_artifact(s)`. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Misuses `log_time_series_metrics` to log input dataset features instead of step-wise loss metrics, omits the required Vertex AI TensorBoard instance, and contains an invalid `log_merrics` method name. • B: Misinterprets `log_time_series_metrics` as a dataset artifact logger rather than a TensorBoard step-metric logger, and omits associating a Vertex AI TensorBoard instance (causing `log_time_series_metrics` to fail). • D: Misuses `log_time_series_metrics` to track preprocessed input data instead of linking dataset artifacts via `assign_input_artifact(s)`.
  • × A Incorrectly uses `log_time_series_metrics` for preprocessed data instead of `assign_input_artifact`, omits associating a TensorBoard instance, and uses `log_metrics` (with a typo) for step-wise loss.
  • × B Incorrectly uses `log_time_series_metrics` to track dataset artifacts instead of `assign_input_artifact`, and `log_metrics` is only for scalar summary metrics rather than step-wise loss curves.
  • × D Incorrectly uses `log_time_series_metrics` to track preprocessed data instead of `assign_input_artifact`, and `log_metrics` logs summary scalars rather than step-by-step loss values.

You recently deployed a model to a Vertex AI endpoint and set up online serving in Vertex AI Feature Store. You have configured a daily batch ingestion job to update your featurestore. During the batch ingestion jobs, you discover that CPU utilization is high in your featurestore’s online serving nodes and that feature retrieval latency is high. You need to improve online serving performance during the daily batch ingestion. What should you do?

✓ Option A: Schedule an increase in the number of online serving nodes in your featurestore prior to the batch ingestion jobs
• Option B: Enable autoscaling of the online serving nodes in your featurestore
• Option C: Enable autoscaling for the prediction nodes of your DeployedModel in the Vertex AI endpoint

Schedule a programmatic increase in the number of Feature Store online serving nodes prior to daily batch ingestion jobs (and scale back down afterward) to absorb the write load without degrading online read latency.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Google Cloud AI/ML Docs (Vertex AI Feature Store — Online Serving Node Scaling & Batch Ingestion Best Practices) & PMLE Study Guide v2.0 Sec 4.2
✅ Why A is Correct: Batch ingestion (`ImportFeatureValues`) writes directly into the same Feature Store online serving nodes that handle live low-latency reads, consuming node CPU. Because online serving node autoscaling reacts slowly (taking up to 20 minutes to provision and rebalance data) and cannot absorb predictable sudden ingestion spikes, Google Cloud recommends scheduling a proactive node-count increase prior to the daily batch ingestion job (and scaling back down afterward). ❌ Why Others Fail: • B: Reactive autoscaling lags behind sudden batch-write CPU bursts while nodes provision and rebalance, still causing elevated online retrieval latency at the start of every daily job. • C: Scaling `DeployedModel` prediction nodes on the Vertex AI Endpoint only adds model-inference compute and does nothing to relieve CPU saturation inside Feature Store's online serving nodes. • D: Increasing `worker_count` on `ImportFeatureValues` drives even higher concurrent write throughput against the online serving nodes, worsening CPU saturation and read latency.
  • × B Vertex AI Feature Store online serving nodes do not support automatic autoscaling to absorb sudden batch ingestion spikes.
  • × C Autoscaling the Vertex AI Endpoint's model prediction nodes does not relieve CPU contention on the Feature Store's online serving nodes.
  • × D Increasing `worker_count` in `ImportFeatureValues` increases ingestion write parallelism, which further saturates online serving node CPU and worsens retrieval latency.

Deploy the newly retrained model to the existing Vertex AI endpoint, use native traffic splitting to route 5% of production traffic to it, and gradually increase traffic as end-user listening metrics improve.

Routing 5% of live traffic to the newly retrained model while monitoring online business KPIs (such as user listening time) before gradually ramping traffic achieves a safe canary/A/B rollout with zero custom routing infrastructure. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Provisioning a second Vertex AI Endpoint and building a custom traffic-splitting proxy microservice duplicates native Vertex AI Endpoint traffic splitting and increases operational complexity. • B: Offline batch predictions on historical logged requests cannot measure real-time interactive user feedback (whether a user actually listens to the newly recommended song). • D: Immediately cutting 100% of production traffic over to the new model exposes all users to potential recommendation regressions, and prediction drift alerts do not measure user engagement quality.

You plan to use Vertex AI's hypertuning service with a budget to perform 100 trials. You want to identify the model architecture and hyperparameter values that minimize training loss and maximize model performance. What should you do?

• Option A: Run one hypertuning job for 100 trials. Set num_hidden_layers as a conditional hyperparameter based on its parent hyperparameter training_method, and set learning_rate as a non-conditional hyperparameter.
• Option B: Run two separate hypertuning jobs, a linear regression job for 50 trials, and a DNN job for 50 trials. Compare their final performance on a common validation set, and select the set of hyperparameters with the least training loss.
• Option C: Run one hypertuning job with training_method as the hyperparameter for 50 trials. Select the architecture with the lowest training loss, and further hypertune it and its corresponding hyperparameters tor 50 trials.

Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Run a single 100-trial Vertex AI hyperparameter tuning job where both `num_hidden_layers` and `learning_rate` are defined as conditional hyperparameters dependent on `training_method`.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #2 (PMLE Study Guide v2.0, Sec 3.3) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Docs: Vertex AI Hyperparameter Tuning Conditional Hyperparameters)
✅ Why D is Correct: Vertex AI Hyperparameter Tuning supports hierarchical `conditionalParameterSpecs`; setting both DNN-only arguments (`num_hidden_layers` and `learning_rate`) as child hyperparameters conditioned on parent `training_method='dnn'` in a single 100-trial job prevents wasting linear-regression trials on inactive DNN parameters. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Leaving `learning_rate` non-conditional forces Vizier to vary `learning_rate` even when `training_method` selects the linear regression model that ignores it, wasting trial budget. • B: Hard-splitting into two 50-trial jobs wastes half the budget tuning a linear regression method that has neither `learning_rate` nor `num_hidden_layers` to tune, and selecting by training loss risks overfitting. • C: Spending 50 trials tuning only `training_method` without tuning the DNN's `learning_rate` and `num_hidden_layers` yields poorly tuned DNN trials that distort architecture selection.
  • × A Leaving `learning_rate` non-conditional wastes trials varying `learning_rate` when `training_method` is set to linear regression, which ignores that argument.
  • × B Splitting the budget into two fixed 50-trial jobs prevents Vertex AI Vizier from dynamically allocating more trials to the more promising architecture.
  • × C Spending 50 trials tuning only `training_method` without tuning DNN hyperparameters unfairly evaluates the DNN with default parameters.

Source: Source #2 (PMLE Study Guide v2.0, Sec 6.2: Monitoring for Feature Attribution Drift) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Docs: Vertex AI Monitor Feature Attributions)
✅ Why D is Correct: Feature attribution drift monitoring uses Vertex Explainable AI Shapley values to detect shifts in feature importances and interactions affecting model predictions, while a `0.1` (10%) request sampling rate on a weekly schedule minimizes Explainable AI compute costs. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Input feature drift monitoring checks univariate input distributions rather than feature importance/interactions, and a `1` (100%) sampling rate maximizes logging cost. • B: Basic feature drift monitoring only tracks statistical shifts in individual raw inputs and neither reveals feature importance nor detects changing feature interactions. • C: Setting the sampling rate to `1` computes expensive Shapley feature attributions on 100% of prediction traffic, violating the requirement to minimize cost.
  • × A Feature drift only monitors raw input distributions rather than feature importances/interactions, and a sampling rate of 1 (100%) maximizes compute cost.
  • × B Feature drift monitoring tracks univariate input distribution shifts rather than calculating feature attributions to monitor feature importance and interactions.
  • × C Setting the sampling rate to 1 (100% of incoming requests) incurs 10x higher attribution compute costs than a 0.1 sampling rate.

Train a BigQuery ML linear regression model using one-hot encoded categorical features and extracted calendar date features such as day of the week and month.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #4 (Google ML Crash Course: Categorical & Numerical Data Feature Engineering) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Docs: BigQuery ML Preprocessing Functions)
✅ Why A is Correct: One-hot encoding unordered categorical features (`store location`, `product category`) avoids false ordinality, while extracting cyclical calendar features (`day of week`, `month`) from `date` exposes retail seasonality so a BigQuery ML linear regression model can accurately predict sales. ❌ Why Others Fail: • B: Arbitrary integer label encoding imposes false numeric ordering on nominal categories, and converting `date` into raw monotonic numbers obscures recurring weekly and monthly seasonality. • C: Autoencoders are unsupervised representation-learning/anomaly-detection models that cannot perform supervised product sales regression. • D: Matrix factorization is designed for collaborative filtering over user-item pairs rather than multi-feature retail sales forecasting with dates and promotions.
  • × B Converting dates into raw numeric timestamps fails to capture cyclical weekly/monthly seasonality, and label encoding imposes arbitrary ordinal rankings on categorical features.
  • × C An autoencoder is an unsupervised neural network used for dimensionality reduction and anomaly detection, not supervised sales forecasting.
  • × D Matrix factorization is designed for collaborative filtering recommendation systems (user-item pairs) rather than tabular sales regression.

Q#314 Sec 2: Data & Collab
Model Development
training a large-scale deep learning model on a Cloud TPUTPU utilization is consistently lowdelays between the completion of one training step and the start of the next step
Clue: Idle gaps between training steps indicate the accelerator (TPU) is starving while waiting for the CPU host to prepare the next batch, which is solved by overlapping CPU preprocessing and TPU execution via `tf.data.Dataset.prefetch`.
View Full Question & 4 Options

You are training a large-scale deep learning model on a Cloud TPU. While monitoring the training progress through Tensorboard, you observe that the TPU utilization is consistently low and there are delays between the completion of one training step and the start of the next step. You want to improve TPU utilization and overall training performance. How should you address this issue?

• Option A: Apply tf.data.Detaset.map with vectorized operations and parallelization.
• Option B: Use tf.data.Detaset.interleave with multiple data sources.
• Option C: Use tf.data.Detaset.cache on the dataset after the first epoch.
✓ Option D: Implement tf.data.Detaset.prefetch in the data pipeline.
Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Add `tf.data.Dataset.prefetch` to the end of the input pipeline so the host CPU prepares the next batch of data in parallel while the TPU executes the current training step.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide, Sec 3.3) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Docs: Cloud TPU Performance Guide & `tf.data.Dataset.prefetch`)
✅ Why D is Correct: Low TPU utilization with idle gaps between consecutive steps indicates the TPU is stalled waiting on the CPU host for input batches; adding `tf.data.Dataset.prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)` overlaps host CPU data preparation for step `N+1` with TPU execution of step `N`. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Vectorized/parallel `Dataset.map` speeds up CPU transformations within a step, but without `prefetch` host preprocessing and TPU execution still run sequentially with inter-step stalls. • B: `Dataset.interleave` parallelizes I/O reads across multiple source files but does not decouple producer CPU execution from consumer TPU step execution. • C: `Dataset.cache` can exhaust host memory on large-scale datasets, does nothing during the first epoch, and still leaves host-to-device delivery unpipelined without `prefetch`.
  • × A Vectorizing and parallelizing `map` speeds up CPU transformation time, but without `prefetch`, the TPU still waits synchronously between steps while the CPU prepares the next batch.
  • × B `interleave` parallelizes reading from multiple files in storage, which addresses I/O throughput rather than overlapping CPU step preparation with TPU step execution.
  • × C Caching a massive dataset in memory can exhaust host RAM and still does not overlap batch delivery with TPU execution between steps.

✅ Why B is Correct: Vertex Explainable AI feature attributions quantify the positive or negative marginal contribution of every input feature (including demographic and potential proxy features) to individual and aggregate fraud predictions, giving stakeholders direct insight into model decision-making and fairness. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Simply dropping explicit demographic columns via Feature Store ('fairness through unawareness') neither explains existing model decisions nor prevents bias through correlated proxy features. • C: Vertex AI Model Monitoring detects statistical skew or drift over time in production inputs rather than explaining internal feature influence or auditing demographic fairness. • D: Searching embeddings of unfair predictions with Vertex AI Vector Search finds nearest neighbors without revealing which features drove the model's biased decisions.
  • × A Removing demographic features ('fairness through unawareness') does not explain the current model's decision-making process and fails to eliminate bias from correlated proxy features.
  • × C Model Monitoring for training-serving skew detects input data distribution shifts over time rather than explaining how features influence model decisions.
  • × D Vertex AI Vector Search retrieves nearest-neighbor embeddings and cannot quantify feature contributions or explain model decision logic.

View Full Question & 4 Options

You are developing a model to detect fraudulent credit card transactions. You need to prioritize detection, because missing even one fraudulent transaction could severely impact the credit card holder. You used AutoML to train a model on users' profile information and credit card transaction data. After training the initial model, you notice that the model is failing to detect many fraudulent transactions. How should you increase the number of fraudulent transactions that are detected?

• Option A: Add more non-fraudulent examples to the training set.
• Option B: Reduce the maximum number of node hours for training.
• Option C: Increase the probability threshold to classify a fraudulent transaction.
✓ Option D: Decrease the probability threshold to classify a fraudulent transaction.
Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Decrease the classification probability threshold so that transactions with lower predicted fraud probabilities are still flagged as positive, increasing recall.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #3 (Google ML Glossary: Classification Threshold & Recall) & Source #4 (Google ML Crash Course: Classification — Thresholding, Precision, and Recall)
✅ Why D is Correct: Lowering the classification probability threshold classifies more borderline transactions as positive (fraudulent), directly increasing recall (true positive rate) and reducing costly false negatives in high-stakes fraud detection. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Adding more majority-class (non-fraudulent) examples exacerbates class imbalance and biases the classifier even further against flagging fraud. • B: Reducing the maximum AutoML training budget (node hours) restricts architecture search and tuning, potentially degrading overall model recall and AUC. • C: Increasing the probability threshold makes the classifier stricter before flagging fraud, increasing false negatives and missing even more fraudulent transactions.
  • × A Adding more majority-class (non-fraudulent) examples worsens class imbalance and further reduces fraud detection recall.
  • × B Reducing the training budget (node hours) degrades overall model convergence and predictive quality rather than improving recall.
  • × C Increasing the probability threshold makes the classifier more conservative, increasing false negatives and missing even more fraud.

You work at an organization that maintains a cloud-based communication platform that integrates conventional chat, voice, and video conferencing into one platform. The audio recordings are stored in Cloud Storage. All recordings have a 16 kHz sample rate and are more than one minute long. You need to implement a new feature in the platform that will automatically transcribe voice call recordings into text for future applications, such as call summarization and sentiment analysis. How should you implement the voice call transcription feature while following Google-recommended practices?

• Option A: Use the original audio sampling rate, and transcribe the audio by using the Speech-to-Text API with synchronous recognition.
✓ Option B: Use the original audio sampling rate, and transcribe the audio by using the Speech-to-Text API with asynchronous recognition.
• Option C: Downsample the audio recordings to 8 kHz, and transcribe the audio by using the Speech-to-Text API with synchronous recognition.
• Option D: Downsample the audio recordings to 8 kHz, and transcribe the audio by using the Speech-to-Text API with asynchronous recognition.
Final Key: B
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (B)

Preserve the native 16 kHz sampling rate for maximum transcription accuracy and use the Speech-to-Text API asynchronous recognition method for recordings longer than one minute.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #2 (PMLE Study Guide v2.0, Sec 1.2: Pre-trained APIs) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Docs: Cloud Speech-to-Text Best Practices & Asynchronous Recognition)
✅ Why B is Correct: Google Speech-to-Text recommends preserving the native 16 kHz wideband sampling rate for optimal recognition accuracy, and requires asynchronous recognition (`LongRunningRecognize` / BatchRecognize) for Cloud Storage audio recordings exceeding 60 seconds. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Synchronous recognition (`Recognize`) rejects audio requests longer than 1 minute (60 seconds). • C: Downsampling 16 kHz audio to 8 kHz discards speech frequencies between 4 kHz and 8 kHz (degrading accuracy), and synchronous recognition fails on audio longer than 1 minute. • D: Downsampling clean 16 kHz recordings to narrowband 8 kHz unnecessarily discards acoustic detail and violates Speech-to-Text audio fidelity best practices.
  • × A Synchronous recognition in Speech-to-Text has a strict 60-second audio duration limit and fails on recordings over one minute.
  • × C Downsampling from 16 kHz to 8 kHz degrades acoustic quality and synchronous recognition fails on audio longer than one minute.
  • × D Downsampling audio from 16 kHz to 8 kHz discards frequency information and violates Google best practices for transcription accuracy.

The model correctly answers questions about the language, but it consistently fails to generate syntactically correct code snippets, often hallucinating Python-like syntax instead. What should you do?

✓ Option B: Use the Agent Platform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) service with a dataset of valid MechScript examples.

• Option D: Copy the MechScript manual into the system prompt using Gemini’s context window.
Final Key: B

Run supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Gemini using a dataset of valid MechScript prompt-code pairs so the model updates its weights to internalize the unseen grammar and syntax.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide §1.2, §3.2) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Agent Platform Supervised Fine-Tuning Docs)
✅ Why B is Correct: While RAG supplies factual reference context, base LLMs lack pre-training token distributions for strictly private domain-specific languages like MechScript; Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on valid MechScript code examples updates model weights to reliably generate valid syntax rather than defaulting to Python patterns. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Increasing temperature increases token sampling randomness, worsening syntactic hallucinations in code generation. • C: Retrieving more RAG chunks does not resolve token-level grammar bias when the model already retrieves factual answers accurately. • D: Stuffing the entire reference manual into every system prompt consumes massive input tokens per query and still fails to override strong pre-trained Python syntax priors as effectively as SFT.
  • × A Increasing temperature increases output randomness and will worsen syntax hallucinations.
  • × C Retrieving more reference manual chunks via RAG provides factual descriptions but cannot teach an LLM to reliably generate a complex unseen code syntax.
  • × D Stuffing the entire manual into the system prompt consumes the context window on every call and still fails to prevent Python-style syntax hallucinations.

✅ Why B is Correct: Decoupling continuous training (scheduled every 30 days) from batch inference (scheduled daily using serverless batch prediction jobs) follows Google Cloud MLOps best practices, keeping each pipeline modular and paying for compute only during job execution. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Embedding a 30-day training cadence inside a daily prediction pipeline via day-counter conditionals tightly couples failure domains and complicates pipeline scheduling/retries. • C: Hosting an always-on online Agent Platform endpoint just to serve once-daily replenishment batch predictions wastes continuous VM/accelerator hours. • D: Retraining the model every single day when fresh retraining is only needed every 30 days wastes ~30x training compute costs.

You are developing a Gemini-based onboarding chatbot to answer users’ questions based on five PDF onboarding documents in Cloud Storage. The documents are updated weekly or monthly as needed. You expect that the application will receive high-volume, repeated user queries against this documentation context. You need to use the most appropriate and cost-effective solution for managing the context and ensuring that the chatbot has up-to-date information. What should you do?

• Option A: Fine-tune a Gemini model using the text from the five PDF files as a training dataset.
• Option B: Send requests with the five PDF files as content pointing to the URI file. Use implicit context caching.
✓ Option C: Create an explicit context cache using the five PDF files, and regenerate the cache when the source files change.
• Option D: Create an explicit context cache using the five PDF files. Set a time-to-live (TTL) of seven days, and regenerate the cache every seven days.
Final Key: C
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (C)

Create an explicit context cache containing the five PDF documents and regenerate the cache automatically whenever the source PDFs in Cloud Storage are updated.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide §1.2) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Gemini Context Caching Overview Docs)
✅ Why C is Correct: Explicit context caching via the Gemini API guarantees token cost and latency savings across high-volume repeated queries against the five PDF documents, while regenerating the explicit cache specifically when source PDFs change ensures responses are never stale and avoids unnecessary cache rebuilds. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Fine-tuning is unsuitable for memorizing factual documents that update weekly/monthly and incurs high repeated training costs. • B: Implicit caching evicts prefixes opportunistically (expiring within <=24 hours) without deterministic cache-hit guarantees or explicit invalidation control. • D: A rigid 7-day TTL serves outdated onboarding answers whenever documents are updated mid-week and wastes rebuild costs when documents remain unchanged for a month.
  • × A Fine-tuning is designed for adapting style/behavior, not memorizing factual document contents that change weekly or monthly.
  • × B Passing the PDF URIs on every request with only implicit caching does not guarantee cache hits and incurs higher input token billing if requests are spread out.
  • × D Regenerating the cache on a fixed 7-day timer risks serving stale onboarding information if documents are updated mid-week.

View Full Question & 4 Options

You are training a ResNet-50 computer vision model on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform using a custom PyTorch container. The training job is configured with a generic machine type and one NVIDIA A100 GPU. During the training, you monitor the resource utilization charts. You observe that the GPU utilization is volatile, frequently dropping to 0% for short intervals, while the CPU utilization remains consistently above 90%. You want to maximize GPU utilization to reduce training time. What should you do?

• Option A: Increase the training batch size to saturate the GPU memory.
✓ Option B: Update the DataLoader utility to increase the num_workers parameter and enable pin_memory.
• Option C: Switch to a machine type with a higher number of GPUs, and implement the torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel strategy in the training code.
• Option D: Enable automatic mixed precision (AMP) to speed up the matrix multiplications.
Final Key: B
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (B)

Increase `num_workers` and enable `pin_memory` in the PyTorch `DataLoader` so CPU workers asynchronously prefetch and transfer image batches to the GPU without stalling it.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide §3.2, §3.3) & Source #2 (PMLE Study Guide v2.0 §3.2, §6.2)
✅ Why B is Correct: GPU utilization oscillating down to 0% while CPU stays >90% is the classic signature of host-side data-loading starvation; increasing num_workers in PyTorch DataLoader parallelizes asynchronous batch prefetching across CPU workers and pin_memory=True accelerates page-locked DMA transfers to the A100 GPU. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Increasing batch size increases GPU memory usage without accelerating per-image CPU decoding or host-to-device data prefetching. • C: Adding more GPUs with DistributedDataParallel accelerates device compute while exacerbating the existing CPU data-pipeline bottleneck. • D: Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) speeds up A100 Tensor Core math on the GPU, causing the GPU to finish batches even faster and wait longer at 0% on the CPU DataLoader.
  • × A Increasing the batch size makes each CPU data-loading stall even longer and does not parallelize CPU data preprocessing.
  • × C Adding more GPUs with `DistributedDataParallel` when a single GPU is already starving for data from the CPU only wastes more GPU resources.
  • × D Automatic mixed precision (AMP) accelerates GPU matrix math, which makes the GPU finish even faster and wait longer on the CPU bottleneck.

View Full Question & 4 Options

You are optimizing the training of a 175-billion parameter LLM on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. You have provisioned a TPU v5p Pod slice with 32 chips for the job. You initially ran the training using standard data parallelism, but the job immediately failed with an out-of-memory (OOM) error. You need to implement a training strategy that resolves the memory issue and minimizes training latency. What should you do?

• Option A: Configure the training to use a parameter server architecture where the model weights are stored in the host CPU memory.
• Option B: Enable gradient checkpointing, and continue using the data parallelism strategy.
✓ Option C: Configure the training to shard the model parameters and optimizer states, and continue using the data parallelism strategy.
• Option D: Scale up the TPU Pod slice to include more chips, and continue using the data parallelism strategy.
Final Key: C
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (C)

Shard the model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across the TPU chips (e.g., via Fully Sharded Data Parallelism / ZeRO) while continuing data-parallel training across the Pod slice.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide §3.3) & Source #5 (Google Cloud TPU v5p Architecture & FSDP/GSPMD Sharding Docs)
✅ Why C is Correct: A 175B-parameter LLM requires ~2.8 TB for weights, gradients, and Adam optimizer states, exceeding a single TPU v5p chip's 95 GiB HBM under pure data parallelism; sharding parameters and optimizer states across all 32 chips (~3.04 TiB aggregate HBM via FSDP/GSPMD over high-speed ICI) eliminates per-chip OOM while preserving data-parallel throughput and low latency. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Offloading weights to host CPU parameter servers bottlenecks every step on slow host-device transfers and ignores TPU Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) collective sharding. • B: Gradient checkpointing only reduces activation memory; replicating ~2.8 TB of unsharded parameters and optimizer states on each 95 GiB chip still immediately OOMs. • D: Adding more TPU chips under unsharded data parallelism still replicates the full 175B model state onto every individual 95 GiB chip, failing with the exact same OOM error.
  • × A Offloading weights to host CPU parameter servers over PCIe introduces severe communication latency that bottlenecks TPU v5p compute.
  • × B Gradient checkpointing only reduces activation memory; a 175B model's weights and optimizer states (>2 TB) still exceed a single TPU v5p chip's 95 GB HBM under standard data parallelism.
  • × D Adding more TPU chips with pure data parallelism still replicates the full 175B model state onto every single chip, immediately failing with the same OOM error.

• Option D: Locate the WhisperX model in the Model Garden and use the “1-click deploy” feature to deploy it to an Agent Platform endpoint. Route the output to a Dataflow pipeline that uses a custom DoFn function to handle the post-processing and logging.
Final Key: C
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (C)

Package the WhisperX model weights, Hugging Face libraries, and proprietary Python diarization post-processing scripts into a single custom serving container and deploy it to a GPU-enabled Vertex AI (Agent Platform) Endpoint.

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide §4.1, §4.2) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Vertex AI Custom Container Prediction Docs)
✅ Why C is Correct: Bundling the PyTorch WhisperX weights, Hugging Face libraries, and proprietary speaker-diarization post-processing into a single custom serving container on a GPU-enabled Agent Platform Endpoint executes inference and post-processing in-process, eliminating extra network hops while providing managed GPU autoscaling. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: Prebuilt PyTorch containers lack custom WhisperX/Hugging Face system dependencies, and forwarding outputs to a separate Cloud Run function adds network serialization latency. • B: Operating a self-managed GKE cluster and HPA introduces unnecessary Kubernetes administration compared to a managed GPU Agent Platform Endpoint. • D: Routing synchronous audio endpoint predictions into an Apache Beam Dataflow pipeline adds streaming window/worker overhead that degrades near-real-time latency.
  • × A Offloading post-processing to a separate Cloud Run function introduces an extra network hop and serialization overhead that increases near-real-time latency.
  • × B Self-managing a GKE cluster and HPA adds unnecessary Kubernetes operational overhead when a managed GPU Vertex AI Endpoint supports custom containers.
  • × D 1-click deploy in Model Garden does not include your proprietary post-processing code, and routing through Dataflow adds streaming pipeline latency.

You deployed a conversational application that uses Gemini. You recently collected thousands of rows of user feedback about the verbosity and accuracy of the model’s responses. The feedback indicated that the responses are factually correct but users want different levels of verbosity depending on the type of question. You need to adjust the model to return responses that are more consistent with users’ expectations. You want to use a scalable solution and minimize application maintenance. What should you do?

• Option A: Experiment with other models in Model Garden. Perform A/B testing by setting each model as your application’s default model. Choose a model based on the results.
• Option B: Ask users to indicate all scenarios where they expect concise responses versus verbose responses. Modify the application’s prompt to include these scenarios and their respective verbosity levels. Re-evaluate the verbosity of responses with updated prompts.
• Option C: Implement a keyword-based routing layer. If the user’s input contains the words “detailed” or “description,” return a verbose response. If the user’s input contains the word “fact,” re-prompt Gemini to summarize the response and return a concise response.
✓ Option D: Ask users to provide examples of responses with the appropriate verbosity as a list of question and answer pairs. Use this dataset to perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in Agent Platform. Re-evaluate the verbosity of responses with the tuned version.
Final Key: D
✓ NB = Gemini = Vote (D)

Curate question-and-answer examples reflecting the desired verbosity levels and run supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Gemini in Vertex AI (Agent Platform).

📓 Grounded Source & Full Rationale
Source: Source #1 (PMLE June 2026 Exam Guide §1.2, §3.2) & Source #5 (Google Cloud Agent Platform Gemini Supervised Fine-Tuning Docs)
✅ Why D is Correct: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Gemini in Agent Platform using curated question-and-answer demonstration pairs teaches the model nuanced, question-type-dependent verbosity directly in its adapted weights, scaling cleanly with minimal ongoing prompt or routing maintenance. ❌ Why Others Fail: • A: A/B testing other untuned Model Garden foundation models will not align any model to your users' specific context-dependent verbosity expectations. • B: Soliciting and hardcoding every conceivable scenario into a massive system prompt bloats per-request input tokens/latency and becomes brittle to maintain. • C: Keyword routing ('detailed', 'fact') fails on natural conversational phrasing and doubles latency/cost by issuing second summarization LLM calls.
  • × A A/B testing other base models in Model Garden will not align responses with your users' specific question-type verbosity expectations.
  • × B Maintaining an ever-growing list of verbosity scenarios inside the application prompt bloats context tokens and becomes brittle to maintain.
  • × C Keyword-based routing on words like 'detailed' or 'fact' fails whenever users phrase questions without those exact trigger words and adds extra LLM calls.
